sections.t: Saudi Arabia lost both of its roads around the Strait of Hormuz in thirty hours: drones from Iraq's Maysan province shut the East-West pipeline carrying four to five million barrels a day to Yanbu, and Houthi forces took Perim island at the mouth of Bab al-Mandab. Mohammed bin Salman asked Washington twice for strikes on the Houthis and was refused twice, receiving intelligence and targeting data instead.

The pipeline is not the story; the answer is. Since 1945 the bargain has been security for oil priced in dollars, on an unstated term: the guarantor defends the flow. Name the mechanism, the GUARANTEE LADDER - weapons, intelligence, escorts, and at the top, killing people who attack you. Clients assume they bought all of it; they bought only the rungs the guarantor's own interest will pay for. Riyadh reached for the top and was handed the third. Glenn Snyder's alliance security dilemma: a junior partner reads what its patron REFUSES more carefully than what it promises.

sections.h: Deep history I - when protection becomes tribute
sections.t: The oldest version of this ladder was built at Delos in 478 BC. The league was voluntary, aimed at Persia, and members could contribute ships or money. Most chose money, because money was convenient and crews were not. In 454 BC the treasury moved from Delos to Athens; phoros stopped meaning subscription and started meaning tribute, and some of it paid for the Parthenon. Thucydides records what became of members who tried to leave: Naxos around 470 and Thasos in 465 were besieged by the fleet they had helped finance. The guarantor prices the guarantee, and the price rises - but the sharper lesson is that the client's own convenience builds the cage. Those allies were disarmed by their preference for paying cash.

sections.h: Deep history II - real, and empty
sections.t: On 31 March 1939 Neville Chamberlain rose in the Commons and guaranteed Poland. It was formalised on 25 August as the Anglo-Polish Agreement of Mutual Assistance, carrying a secret protocol - published only after the war - that restricted the British obligation to aggression by Germany alone. So when the Red Army crossed on 17 September, Britain owed Poland precisely nothing. War was declared on 3 September; the French pushed a few miles into the Warndt forest and withdrew; Poland was finished in five weeks. The guarantee was legally genuine, publicly made and militarily undeliverable - honoured in declaration, void in relief, with the fine print written where the client could not read it.

sections.h: Deep history III - the hostage solution
sections.t: NATO was the attempt to fix that, and Article 5 repays reading slowly. Members assist by taking "such action as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force" - twelve lines where the Brussels Treaty's Article IV took four, because the US Senate would not sign automaticity. The famous clause is weaker than the clause it replaced. What made it hold for seventy-seven years was not text but Thomas Schelling's insight in Arms and Influence (1966): you cannot make a promise credible by asserting it, only by removing your own choice. American troops in West Germany and Korea, with their families, were no defence - at the Fulda Gap they would have been overrun in days. They were hostages, and a tripwire converts a future decision into an automatic consequence. Credibility bought with bodies, not adjectives. De Gaulle asked anyway - would Washington trade New York for Paris? - and answered himself with the force de frappe in 1960.

sections.h: Deep history IV - from the Quincy to Abqaiq
sections.t: On 14 February 1945, returning from Yalta, Roosevelt met Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake. The ladder went up from there: the 1974 recycling arrangements; the Carter Doctrine of 23 January 1980, declaring an assault on the Gulf would be "repelled by any means necessary"; CENTCOM in 1983; half a million American soldiers deployed for a client state in 1991. The top rung was climbed exactly once. Then 14 September 2019: missiles and drones hit Abqaiq and Khurais and removed 5.7 million barrels a day, over half of Saudi production. The president said America was "locked and loaded," did nothing, and explained why in the sentence that has governed the Gulf ever since - that was an attack on Saudi Arabia, and it wasn't an attack on us. Seven years of Saudi behaviour follow: the Beijing-brokered normalisation with Tehran in 2023, and on 17 September 2025 the Saudi-Pakistan Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed with a nuclear-armed state and left deliberately vague on whether the arsenal is included. Pakistan's defence minister said the capability "will be made available," then walked it back. The ambiguity is not sloppiness. It is the French move, performed by a client who has learned how credibility gets manufactured.

Guarantees decay from the top down: you stop striking before you stop deploying, and stop deploying before you stop selling. The rung that survives serves the guarantor's own interest - Washington kept the lane open, an American problem, and declined the land war behind it. Clients rarely defect; they dilute. Where it breaks: in 1939 Britain wanted to help and could not, in 2026 America can and will not.

Mearsheimer holds that commitments bind only where the guarantor's own survival is engaged; everything else is cheap talk - the logic of his 1993 case for Ukraine keeping its warheads. Ikenberry holds that institutionalised orders outlive the power that built them. Mearsheimer takes WHICH rungs held: the US defended the commons it consumes, not the war it doesn't. Ikenberry takes why there was no rupture: Riyadh took the intelligence and stayed. Then Schelling against Mearsheimer on the remedy - Article 5 has held over Estonia, where no American survival interest exists, because American battalions stand on it. Schelling wins the mechanism, Mearsheimer the forecast that nobody will station a tripwire in Yemen. Sagan supplies the falsifiable consequence: states build when someone else's guarantee loses credibility, not when the threat rises.

The US produces some 13.8 million barrels a day, and near eighty per cent of Hormuz crude goes to Asia: American hulls escort Chinese and Indian barrels. That subsidy to a rival will not survive twenty years of fiscal stress in a country whose debt service exceeds its defence budget - Kennedy's overstretch, or more precisely Gilpin's rising protection costs. By 2035 the American Gulf posture converts from insurance into a fee-and-arms business: about 60 per cent. Bolder: at least one Gulf state holds an overt or thinly-veiled latent nuclear capability by 2035, about 55 per cent. Our twelve-month ledger line on a Saudi announcement is 21 per cent, and a floor: hedging is covert, so watch reactor tenders for a fuel-cycle clause. Counterweight: announced after Suez and after Saigon too. Disconfirmers: US strikes on the Houthis within sixty days, or a ratified treaty with Riyadh.

Glenn Snyder, Alliance Politics (1997) - the abandonment-entrapment dilemma. - Thomas Schelling, Arms and Influence (1966), ch. 2-3 - why a tripwire beats a treaty. - Scott Sagan, "Why Do States Build Nuclear Weapons?" (International Security, 1996).
